extracted.intended_audience: advanced students, mathematicians and physicists studying classical (Newtonian) mechanics and geometrical derivations of orbital motion
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric derivations and construction problems relating centripetal forces to orbital motion (areas, velocities, periods) and explicit force-laws for circular, elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic and spiral trajectories, plus constructions to find centres and orbits from given data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem I — Areas proportional to times
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas quas corpora in gyros acta radiis ad immobile centrum virium ductis describunt, & in planis immobilibus consistere, & esse temporibus proportionales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by dividing time into equal parts: if centripetal impulses act at discrete instants the areas described about the center in equal times are equal; taking the limit as the subdivisions become infinite gives that the areas described in any times are proportional to those times. Corol.1: in nonresisting media, if areas are not proportional to times then forces do not tend to the centers of the radii. Corol.2: if area description accelerates, forces do not tend to the centers but deviate accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem II — Areas proportional imply centripetal force
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus omne quod, cum movetur in linea aliqua curva, & radio ducto ad punctum vel immobile, vel motu rectilineo uniformiter progrediens, describit areas circa punctum illud temporibus proportionales, urgetur a vi centripeta tendente ad idem punctum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Converse of Theorem I: if a body moving in a curve with radii to a point describes areas proportional to times, then the force acting to produce the deflection from rectilinear motion acts along lines directed to that point. Cases and scholium note composition of centripetal forces from multiple components and the irrelevance of perpendicular components to surface motion for area description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem III — Composite forces and area law for two-body interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus omne quod, radio ad centrum corporis alterius uctunq; moti ducto, describit areas circa centrum illud temporibus proportionales, urgetur vi composita ex vi centripeta tendente ad corpus alterum & ex vi omni acceleratrice, qua corpus alterum urgetur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a body describes areas about another body with radii to it proportional to times, then the net force on the first is the composition of the centripetal force toward the second and any accelerative force acting on the second body. Corollaries: removing (by composition) the accelerative part leaves the remaining force tending to the other body as centre; near-proportionality implies near-tendency, and vice versa. Scholium: equal-area description is an index of the centre which the predominant force respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem IV — Centripetal forces for circular motion (v^2/r relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporum quæ diversos circulos æquabili motu describunt, vires centripetas ad centra eorundem circulorum tendere, & esse inter se ut arcuum simul descriptorum quadrata applicata ad circulorum radios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the polygonal approximation the result yields the familiar proportion that centripetal forces are in the ratio of the squares of the velocities applied to the radii; corollaries rephrase: forces ∝ velocity^2 / radius and relations in terms of period (squares of periods applied to radii). Additional corollaries give special cases (equal periods, equal radii etc.) and a scholium relates these proportions to gravitational and centrifugal forces and to limiting polygonal reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem I — Find centre from given velocities (geometric construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data quibuscunq; in locis velocitate, qua corpus figuram datam viribus ad commune aliquod centrum tendentibus describit, centrum illud invenire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: tangent the given curve at three points P,Q,R; erect perpendiculars PA, QB, RC proportional reciprocally to velocities at those points; from endpoints draw lines and their intersection gives lines whose intersection is the sought centre S. Proof uses area law to relate perpendiculars to velocities and thereby locate centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem V / Prob. II — Local relation of centripetal force to small geometric elements
rubrics_metrics.description: If a curve APQ is described and at P it is tangented by ZPR, with QR drawn parallel to SP and QT perpendicular to SP, then the centripetal force is reciproce ut solidum SP quad. × QT quad. ÷ QR (taking the limiting solid as Q→P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a local geometric expression for the centripetal force in terms of the small elements SP, QT, QR in the infinitesimal limit. Corollary: from a given curve and a chosen centre the law of the centripetal force that will produce motion along the curve can be found by computing that solid quantity (SP^4 × QT^4 ÷ QR in the page wording).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem II — Centripetal law for motion in a circle toward a point on circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: Gyretur corpus in circumferentia circuli, requiritur lex vis centripetæ tendentis ad punctum aliquod in circumferentia datum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric derivation (using similar triangles) shows the appropriate proportionalities; the argument leads to expressions (in original wording) involving QT^2 ÷ QR ∼ SP^QC terms and eventually concludes on the dependence of the centripetal force on distance. Construction method given in detail in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem III — Centripetal law for circle when distant centre makes radii nearly parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: Moveatur corpus in circulo PQA: ad hunc effectum requiritur lex vis centripetæ tendentis ad punctum adeo longinquum, ut lineæ omnes PS, RS ad id ductæ, pro parallelis haberi possint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using similar triangles and limits, the proposition simplifies to a law where the centripetal force is (in page wording) 'reciproce ut PM cub.' (neglecting a fixed factor), i.e. dependence on the cube of an ordinate; full derivation included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem IV — Centripetal law for spiral
rubrics_metrics.description: Gyretur corpus in spiral PQS secante radios omnes SP, SQ, &c. in angulo dato: Requiritur lex vis centripetæ tendentis ad centrum spiralis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a spiral cutting all radii at a given angle the argument yields that QT^2 ÷ QR is proportional to SP, and via Theorem V gives that the centripetal force is proportional to the cube of the distance SP: 'vis centripeta ut cubus distantiæ SP.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XII — Equal parallelograms about an ellipse (geometric fact used in later proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallelogramma omnia circa datam Ellipsin descripta esse inter se æqualia. Idem intellige de Parallelogmis in Hyperbola circum diametros ejus descriptis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement used to relate rectangular areas and ordinates in conics when constructing force-laws for conic motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem V / Prop. X — Centripetal law for motion in an ellipse (toward centre of ellipse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gyretur corpus in Ellipsi: requiritur lex vis centripetæ tendentis ad centrum Ellipseos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using conic properties and lemmas the proof arrives (in the page wording) at an expression concluding that the centripetal force is 'reciproce ut 1 ÷ PC, hoc est, directe ut distantia PC' (see original passage); corollaries: if force ∝ distance then motion may be an ellipse with the centre of force at the centre of the ellipse, and equal revolution times for similar figures etc. Scholium notes the parabola arises when centre recedes to infinity (Galileo's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem VI / Prop. XI — Centripetal law for motion in ellipse toward its umbilicus (focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolvatur corpus in Ellipsi: Requiritur lex vis centripetæ tendentis ad umbilicum Ellipseos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed geometric construction and algebraic relations using conjugate diameters give that the centripetal force is reciprocally as L × SP^2 (in the page wording) and hence 'reciproce in ratione duplicata distantiæ SP' — i.e. inverse-square dependence relative to distance from the umbilicus (focus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem VII / Prop. XII — Centripetal law for motion in hyperbola toward its umbilicus
rubrics_metrics.description: Moveatur corpus in Hyperbola: requiritur lex vis centripetæ tendentis ad umbilicum figuræ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By analogous argument to the ellipse case (using semiaxes and conjugate diameters) the centripetal force is again shown (per page) to be reciprocally in the duplicate ratio of the distance SP (inverse-square). Conclusion: inverse-square law yields hyperbolic motion when appropriate conditions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XIII & XIV — Geometric properties of conic ordinates and tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma XIII: Latus rectum Parabolæ ad verticem quemvis pertinens, est quadruplum distantiæ verticis illius ab umbilico figuræ. Lemma XIV: Perpendiculum quod ab umbilico Parabolæ ad tangentem ejus demittitur, medium est proportionale inter distantias umbilici a puncto contactus & a vertice principali figuræ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lemmas supply proportional relations between ordinates, focal distances and tangent perpendiculars used in constructing the force-law for parabolic motion (and in subsequent corollaries). Several corollaries give squared and proportional relations used in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem VIII / Prop. XIII — Centripetal law for motion in a parabola (toward its umbilicus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moveatur corpus in perimetro Parabolæ: requiritur Lex vis centripetæ tendentis ad umbilicum hujus figuræ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the previous lemmas and conic properties the proposition demonstrates that the centripetal force is reciprocally as SP^2 (stated in the page as 'reciproce in duplicata ratione distantiæ SP'). Corollaries: many consequences including that if a body on a straight line is simultaneously acted on by inverse-square centripetal force it will move in a conic with a focus at the centre of force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem VI / Prop. XIV — Orbital semilatus and area relation for inverse-square force
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora plura revolvantur circa centrum commune, & vis centripeta decrescat in duplicata ratione distantiarum a centro; dico quod Orbium Latera recta sunt in duplicata ratione arearum quas corpora, radiis ad centrum ductis, eodem tempore describunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If centripetal force obeys inverse-square, then the semilatus rectum L of orbits is in duplicate ratio to the area described about the centre in a given time (i.e. L ∝ (area)^{2}). Corollary: ellipse total area proportional relation to axes and period follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem VII / Prop. XV — Periods in ellipses (Kepler's third law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, dico quod tempora periodica in Ellipsibus sunt in ratione sesquiplicata transversorum axium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives that the periodic times in ellipses are in the 3/2 (sesquiplicate) ratio of the transverse axes (i.e. T ∝ a^{3/2}), following from proportions between semilatus, axes and areas. Corollary: periods in ellipses equal those in circles whose diameters equal the major axes of the ellipses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem VIII / Prop. XVI — Velocity relation via perpendiculars and semilatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, & actis ad corpora lineis rectis, quæ ibidem tangant orbitas, demissisq; ab umbilico communi ad has tangentes perpendicularibus: dico quod velocitates corporum sunt in ratione composita ex ratione perpendiculorum inverse & dimidiata ratione laterum rectorum directe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a composite proportionality for speed: velocity ratios combine the inverse ratio of perpendiculars from the centre to the tangent and the 'dimidiata' (square-root/half-power) ratio of the semilatus (latus rectum) directly. Several corollaries follow concerning velocities at extrema and comparisons between conic sections and circular motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem IX / Prop. XVII — Given inverse-square central force and magnitude, determine orbit from given initial position and velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Posito quod vis centripeta sit reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ a centro, & quod vis illius quantitas absoluta sit cognita; requiritur linea quam corpus describit, de loco dato cum data velocitate secundum datam rectam egrediens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive procedure: from given latus rectum L (determined by local geometric relations to perpendiculars and velocities) and known foci/umbilicus, one can determine whether the resulting conic is ellipse, parabola or hyperbola based on the relation between L and other geometric quantities (2SP+2KP etc.), and thus the full orbit and its orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem X / Prop. XVIII — Construct conic trajectory with given focus and transverse axis through points or tangent lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Datis umbilico & axibus transversis describere Trajectorias Ellipticas & Hyperbolicas, quæ transibunt per puncta data, & rectas positione datas contingent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw circles of radius equal to the transverse axis around chosen centres and locate intersections to define the conic having the given umbilicus and transverse axis and passing through given points or tangents. Proof uses Lemma XV and conic focal properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem XI / Prop. XIX — Construct parabola with given focus through given points or tangent positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Circa datum umbilicum Trajectoriam Parabolicam describere, quæ transibit per puncta data, & rectas positione datas continget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via circles and a perpendicular bisected chord: given focus S, a point P and a tangent TR, draw a circle about P, produce perpendicular from S to tangent, reflect and bisect to find vertex K and hence the parabola with vertex K and focus S that passes through given data. Uses Lemma XIV corollaries to ensure tangent/vertex relations.
